problem: "till she dismissed me, I could not pursue my observations on Miss Scatcherd's movements" is rendered as having "lost track" by the time she was dismissed (a different claim), and Burns "returned in half a minute" is dropped.
new_text: My attention was then diverted by Miss Smith, who asked me to hold a skein of thread while she wound it. As she worked, she chatted with me, asking whether I'd been to school before, whether I could do marking, stitching, knitting, and so on. Until she dismissed me, I couldn't keep watching what Miss Scatcherd was doing. When I returned to my seat, that teacher was just giving an order I didn't catch. But Burns immediately left the class, went into the small inner room where the books were kept, and came back half a minute later carrying a bundle of twigs tied together at one end. She presented this ominous tool to Miss Scatcherd with a respectful curtsy. Then quietly, without being told, she loosened her pinafore, and the teacher instantly struck her a dozen sharp blows on the neck with the bunch of twigs. Not a tear rose to Burns's eye. And while I froze in my sewing, my fingers trembling with helpless, impotent anger at the spectacle, not a feature of her thoughtful face changed its ordinary expression.

problem: Source "I should dislike her; I should resist her" is intensified to "I'd hate her", losing the echo of Helen's "she dislikes my faults".
new_text: "If I were in your place, I'd dislike her. I'd fight back. If she hit me with that rod, I'd grab it out of her hand. I'd break it right in front of her."

problem: Drops the causal clause "for listening to the visionary brook" — she hears nothing because she is listening to the imagined brook.
new_text: "For you, I'm sure it is. I watched you in class this morning and saw how closely you paid attention. Your mind never seemed to wander while Miss Miller explained the lesson and questioned you. But mine constantly drifts. When I should be listening to Miss Scatcherd and absorbing every word, I often lose the very sound of her voice. I fall into a kind of dream. Sometimes I imagine I'm back in Northumberland, and the noises around me are the bubbling of a little brook that runs through Deepden, near our house. Then when it's my turn to answer, I have to be woken up, and having heard nothing of what was read because I was listening to the imaginary brook, I have nothing to say."

problem: Drops Jane's emphatic self-assurance "I am sure we should" and the "very hard" intensity.
new_text: "There's a great deal of it. You're good to those who are good to you. That's all I ever want to be. If people were always kind and obedient to those who are cruel and unjust, the wicked would have everything their way. They'd never feel afraid, so they'd never change—they'd just get worse and worse. When someone hits us for no reason, we should hit back very hard—I'm sure we should—hard enough to teach them never to do it again."

problem: "degradation never too deeply disgusts me, injustice never crushes me too low" is garbled into "degradation never crushes me too deeply, injustice never brings me too low" (loses "disgusts"); also "the time will soon come" loses "soon".
new_text: "She has been unkind to you, no doubt, because she dislikes your personality—just as Miss Scatcherd dislikes mine. But how precisely you remember everything she has done and said to you! What a remarkably deep impression her injustice has made on your heart! No ill-treatment leaves such a record on my feelings. Wouldn't you be happier if you tried to forget her cruelty, along with the angry emotions it stirred up? Life seems too short to me to be spent nursing grudges or cataloguing wrongs. We are all burdened with faults in this world, every one of us. But the time will soon come, I trust, when we shed those faults along with our perishable bodies—when sin and degradation fall away with this heavy frame of flesh, and only the spark of the spirit remains, the intangible essence of light and thought, as pure as when it left the Creator to give life to the creature. Where it came from, it will return—perhaps to be given to some being higher than us, perhaps to pass through levels of glory, from the pale human soul brightening to the radiance of an angel! Surely it will never be allowed to degrade from human to demon? No, I cannot believe that. I hold a different belief, one no one ever taught me, one I rarely speak of, but which gives me joy and which I cling to—because it offers hope to everyone. It makes Eternity a place of rest, a great home, not a terror and an abyss. And with this belief, I can clearly separate the wrongdoer from the wrong. I can sincerely forgive the person while hating the act. With this belief, revenge never torments my heart, degradation never disgusts me too deeply, injustice never crushes me too low. I live in peace, looking toward the end."

She wasn't given much time to reflect, though. A monitor—a big, rough girl—came up and exclaimed in a strong Cumberland accent—

problem: "reserve a moiety" means save half; "save some" loses the proportion (half kept, the rest given up).
new_text: A small consolation came at teatime: a double ration of bread—a whole slice instead of half—with the glorious addition of a thin scraping of butter. This was the weekly treat we all looked forward to from one Sunday to the next. I usually managed to save half of this feast for myself, but the rest I was invariably forced to give away.

problem: The Eutychus allusion is compressed: drops "if not out of the third loft" (Acts 20:9) and "be taken up half dead"; "yawns attested her weariness" becomes "boredom".
new_text: Sunday evenings were spent reciting the Church Catechism and chapters five, six, and seven of St. Matthew by heart, and listening to a long sermon read by Miss Miller, whose irrepressible yawns showed how tired she was. A frequent interruption was half a dozen little girls playing the part of Eutychus: overwhelmed by sleep, they would fall down—if not out of the third loft, then off the fourth bench—and be picked up half dead. The remedy was to push them into the center of the schoolroom and make them stand until the sermon was done. Sometimes their legs gave out and they collapsed in a heap. Then they were propped up with the monitors' tall stools.

problem: Source hedges "perhaps prolonging his stay"; "presumably" raises the certainty.
new_text: I haven't mentioned the visits of Mr. Brocklehurst yet. In fact, that gentleman was away from home for most of the first month after my arrival, perhaps lingering with his friend the Archdeacon. His absence was a relief to me. I need not explain that I had my own reasons for dreading his appearance. But appear he did, at last.

problem: The ironic quoted epithet "Coming Man" (source: looking out daily for the "Coming Man") is dropped and replaced by plain "this man".
new_text: I had my own reasons to be alarmed by this appearance. I remembered all too well Mrs. Reed's treacherous hints about my character, and Mr. Brocklehurst's promise to warn Miss Temple and the teachers about my wicked nature. All along, I had been dreading the fulfillment of that promise—watching daily for the "Coming Man," whose report about my past was going to brand me as a bad child forever. And now here he was.

problem: "vile bodies" is Brocklehurst's scriptural phrase (Philippians 3:21); "worthless bodies" loses the echo.
new_text: "Madam, allow me a moment. You are aware that my purpose in educating these girls is not to accustom them to luxury and indulgence, but to make them hardy, patient, and self-denying. If some small disappointment of appetite occurs, such as a spoiled meal or an under- or over-cooked dish, the proper response is not to replace it with something finer, thereby pampering the body and undermining the purpose of this institution. Rather, the incident should be used for the spiritual improvement of the pupils, by encouraging them to show courage in the face of temporary deprivation. A brief talk on such occasions would be perfectly appropriate, in which a wise teacher might refer to the sufferings of the early Christians, to the torments of martyrs, to the exhortations of our blessed Lord Himself, calling upon His disciples to take up their cross and follow Him—to His warnings that man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God—to His divine comfort: 'If you suffer hunger or thirst for My sake, blessed are you.' Oh, madam, when you put bread and cheese instead of burned porridge into these children's mouths, you may indeed feed their vile bodies, but you little realize how you starve their immortal souls!"

problem: The biblical allusion "the outside of the cup and platter" (Matthew 23:25) is shortened to "the cup", weakening recognition.
new_text: Miss Temple passed her handkerchief across her lips, as if smoothing away an involuntary smile. She gave the order, though, and when the first class understood what was being asked, they obeyed. Leaning back on my bench a little, I could see the looks and grimaces they exchanged. It was a pity Mr. Brocklehurst couldn't see them too—he might have realized that however much he controlled the outside of the cup and platter, the inside was far beyond his reach.

problem: Drops the image "the reverse of these living medals" (the girls as coins/medals turned face-down).
new_text: He scrutinized the reverse side of these living medals—the backs of their heads—for about five minutes, then delivered his verdict. The words fell like a death sentence—

problem: "the Rubicon was passed; and that the trial, no longer to be shirked, must be firmly sustained" becomes "the worst had happened", which is not the source's sense (a point of no return and an ordeal to be endured) and drops the allusion.
new_text: A pause—during which I began to steady my shaking nerves and to feel that the Rubicon was crossed, and that the ordeal, which could no longer be avoided, must be firmly endured.

problem: "as if a martyr, a hero, had passed a slave or victim" loses "martyr" and "victim"; "marked lineaments" (strongly defined features) becomes "plain features"; "the disc of the clearest planet" becomes "the brightest star".
new_text: There I was, raised up high—I, who had said I couldn't bear the shame of standing on my own feet in the middle of the room, was now displayed on a pedestal of disgrace for everyone to see. What I felt, no words can describe. But just as all those feelings rose, choking me and closing my throat, a girl walked past. As she passed, she raised her eyes. What a strange light filled them! What an extraordinary feeling that glance sent through me! How it lifted me up! It was as if a martyr, a hero, had walked past a slave or victim and passed on strength just by being near. I mastered the rising hysteria, raised my head, and stood firm on the stool. Helen Burns asked Miss Smith some trivial question about her work, was scolded for bothering her, returned to her place, and smiled at me as she went by. What a smile! I remember it now, and I know it was the expression of a fine mind and real courage. It lit up her strongly marked features, her thin face, her sunken gray eyes, like the reflection of an angel. Yet at that very moment, Helen Burns wore the "untidy" badge on her arm. Barely an hour ago, I had heard Miss Scatcherd sentence her to a dinner of bread and water the next day for blotting a copying exercise. Such is the imperfect nature of humanity! Such spots exist on the disc of the clearest planet—and eyes like Miss Scatcherd's can only see those tiny flaws, blind to the full brilliance of the whole.

problem: Drops "weakly" from "weakly and pompously repeated" (Helen's judgment of Brocklehurst) and "sovereign" from "the sovereign hand that created your frame".
new_text: "Hush, Jane! You care too much about human love. You are too passionate, too intense. The sovereign hand that made you and gave you life has provided you with other resources besides your own frail self, or other frail creatures like you. Beyond this earth and the human race, there is an invisible world and a kingdom of spirits. That world surrounds us, for it is everywhere. Those spirits watch over us, for they are charged with guarding us. And if we were dying in pain and shame, if scorn attacked us from all sides and hatred crushed us, angels would see our suffering, recognize our innocence (if innocent we are, as I know you are of this charge Mr. Brocklehurst has weakly and pompously repeated secondhand from Mrs. Reed—for I read a sincere nature in your passionate eyes and clear face), and God waits only for the spirit to leave the body to crown us with a full reward. Why, then, should we ever sink into despair, when life is so soon over and death is so certain a gateway to happiness—to glory?"

problem: "she was sorry to have to do it" (reluctant) is sharpened to "She resented having to do it".
new_text: "No, ma'am. She was sorry to have to do it. But my uncle, as I often heard the servants say, made her promise before he died that she would always keep me."

problem: "most moderate—most correct" (restrained and accurate) becomes "careful and fair"; the resolve to be accurate matters since Miss Temple asked her to add and exaggerate nothing.
new_text: I resolved with all my heart to be as moderate and as accurate as possible. After thinking for a few minutes to organize what I had to say, I told her the whole story of my unhappy childhood. Drained by emotion, my language was calmer than it usually was when I talked about that sad subject. And remembering Helen's warnings against giving in to resentment, I put far less bitterness into the account than usual. Restrained and simplified like this, it sounded more believable. I could feel as I went on that Miss Temple fully believed me.

problem: "not the least delight" (litotes: one of the chief pleasures) becomes "the greatest pleasure"; "as on nectar and ambrosia" flattened to "like gods".
new_text: We feasted that evening as if on nectar and ambrosia. And not the least pleasure of the meal was the smile of satisfaction on our hostess's face as she watched us satisfy our starving appetites with the fine food she so generously provided.

problem: Source "bound it like a phylactery" (the scripture case worn on the forehead) is replaced with "like a crown of thorns", an invented Christ-image that changes the allusion.
new_text: The next morning, Miss Scatcherd wrote the word "SLATTERN" in large letters on a piece of cardboard and bound it like a phylactery (a small scripture case worn strapped to the forehead) around Helen's large, gentle, intelligent, kind-looking forehead. She wore it all day, patient and uncomplaining, accepting it as a deserved punishment. The moment Miss Scatcherd left after afternoon classes, I ran to Helen, tore it off, and threw it in the fire. The fury that Helen was incapable of feeling had been burning in my soul all day, and tears—hot, large tears—had been scalding my cheeks continuously, because the sight of her quiet resignation caused me unbearable pain.

problem: "Cuyp-like groups of cattle" loses the painter's name; "translate currently" (fluently) loses the adverb.
new_text: Freed from that crushing weight, I set to work again from that hour, determined to push through every difficulty. I worked hard, and my success matched my effort. My memory, not naturally strong, improved with practice. Exercise sharpened my mind. Within a few weeks I was promoted to a higher class. In less than two months I was allowed to start French and drawing. I learned the first two tenses of the verb etre and sketched my first cottage (whose walls, I should mention, rivaled the leaning tower of Pisa in their slope) on the same day. That night, going to bed, I forgot to fantasize about the imaginary feast of hot roast potatoes or fresh bread and milk that I usually conjured to comfort my hunger. Instead I feasted on visions of ideal drawings, all created by my own hands—freely sketched houses and trees, picturesque rocks and ruins, groups of cattle like those in a Cuyp painting, lovely paintings of butterflies hovering over rosebuds, birds picking ripe cherries, wren's nests holding pearl-like eggs wreathed in young ivy. I also pondered whether I would ever be able to translate fluently a certain little French story that Madame Pierrot had shown me that day. That problem was not solved to my satisfaction before I fell sweetly asleep.

problem: Proverbs 15:17 "a stalled ox and hatred therewith" is altered to "a fattened calf", changing the recognizable scripture (and echoing the prodigal son instead).
new_text: Solomon was right: "Better a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred with it."
